opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the clearest historical cases. When you go back and read the debates over women's suffrage, women's education, or women entering the professions, what's striking is how much of the opposition was framed not as "it's simply wrong for women to vote" but as factual claims about the world. You had arguments that women were constitutionally more emotional and so would vote erratically; that higher education would damage women's reproductive health (there were physicians making literally that claim, that intellectual exertion would divert energy from the reproductive organs); that women would just copy their husbands' votes, so suffrage would change nothing except to cause domestic strife; or that women didn't actually want the vote and the demand came from an unrepresentative fringe.

Those are all empirical claims, and they turned out to be false, sometimes spectacularly. Women went to university in large numbers and there was no reproductive catastrophe. Women voted, and society didn't collapse, families didn't disintegrate.

But the interesting thing is how those claims functioned in the argument. They were doing a lot of the moral work. If you believe women are incapable of reasoned political judgment, then excluding them can look like a benevolent, protective policy rather than an injustice. So the moral conclusion, "it's fine, even good, to deny these rights," rested on a factual foundation that people weren't really scrutinizing as factual. And often the direction of causation seemed to run backwards: people were motivated to hold the existing social arrangement, and the empirical beliefs got recruited to support it. You can see that because when one empirical claim was refuted, a new one would often appear to take its place, while the conclusion stayed fixed.

I think there are a few lessons there. One is that when you see a moral position that's strongly supported by empirical claims that happen to be convenient for the people holding power, and those claims aren't being tested, that's a warning sign. Another is that a lot of moral progress has actually come from empirical correction, from people discovering that the factual premises were wrong, rather than from some deep shift in fundamental values. Many people who opposed suffrage shared values like caring about good governance and family wellbeing. They just had false beliefs about what women were like and what would happen.

And that's relevant to how we should think about our own era. We should ask: where are we bundling moral conclusions with empirical premises that we haven't really examined, and that happen to be convenient for us? That applies to questions about animals and their capacity for suffering, about people in distant countries, about future generations, and potentially about new kinds of minds, like AI systems, where there's enormous motivated reasoning available in either direction. The historical pattern suggests we should separate out the factual questions, investigate them seriously, and be suspicious when our factual beliefs line up a little too neatly with what's comfortable.

fable-5.1.text:
Carl Shulman: Yeah, so one of the things I find really striking when you go back and read the actual arguments people made — say, against women's suffrage, or against women entering higher education or the professions — is how much of the argumentative weight was carried by claims that are, at least in principle, empirical. And they were frequently just false.

So you'd have claims that women lacked the intellectual capacity for political judgment, that higher education would damage women's health or their reproductive capacity — there was this whole genre of medical literature about how the strain of study would divert energy from the reproductive organs. Claims that women were too emotional to be trusted with a vote, that giving them the franchise would destabilise the family, that women themselves didn't actually want it, or that the household already had one vote and the husband represented it adequately. Some of these are moral claims dressed up — like the household-representation one — but a lot of them are straightforwardly predictions about what would happen or descriptions of what women are like.

And the thing is, these were testable, and they got tested. Women went to university and did fine. Women voted and civilisation didn't collapse. In many of the countries that extended the franchise, you can look at what actually happened to policy, to family structure, and the catastrophic predictions just didn't pan out. So in retrospect it looks like the moral position was being propped up by a scaffolding of empirical beliefs that people held with great confidence and that turned out to be wrong.

What I take from that is a kind of methodological lesson. When you have a strong moral intuition and it's accompanied by a bunch of empirical claims that conveniently support it, you should be suspicious that the causal arrow is running backwards — that the moral commitment is generating the empirical beliefs rather than the other way around. People who were comfortable with the existing arrangement found it very easy to believe facts that justified the arrangement. And they weren't, for the most part, obviously stupid or dishonest; they were operating in an information environment where those claims were respectable and where the costs of examining them were high and the benefits low, if you were a man who benefited from the status quo.

And this generalises. Lots of moral questions that look like pure values disagreements actually have a huge empirical component — what are the consequences, what are these beings like, what do they want, what capacities do they have. If you can isolate the empirical parts and actually check them, you'll often find that a disagreement that seemed intractable has a chunk that can be resolved. And historically, when that's happened, the moral conclusion has often shifted pretty dramatically once the false factual beliefs were cleared away. So I think it's worth asking, for our own moral views today, which of them are leaning on empirical claims we haven't really examined, and whether we'd hold them with the same confidence if those claims turned out to be wrong.

astra-6.text:
One thing you see is that opposition to women’s rights was often defended with empirical claims about women’s capacities, or about what would happen to society if women had more freedom. So someone might say that women were incapable of exercising political judgment, or that giving women access to education and careers would cause the family to collapse. Those claims were bundled together with claims about women’s proper role and the authority men ought to have.

And that matters because an empirical disagreement can make a moral disagreement look smaller than it really is. Someone can say, “Of course I care about women’s welfare; I just think these restrictions are necessary for everyone’s good.” Then you can ask: if women could do these things competently, and the predicted harms didn’t occur, would you support equal rights? That helps distinguish how much of the position depends on beliefs about consequences and how much depends on valuing the hierarchy itself.

It also means that changes in practice can provide evidence. Once women are actually participating in education, professions, and politics, claims that they simply cannot do those things become much harder to sustain. That doesn’t by itself settle every moral question, but it can remove an empirical justification that was doing a lot of work in defending an unequal arrangement.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, one recurring pattern is that people defend a social arrangement partly by saying it’s morally appropriate, but also by claiming that departing from it would have terrible consequences. So arguments against women’s rights might appeal to women’s supposed intellectual limitations, or say that political participation would undermine the family and damage society.

Those are empirical claims. They make predictions about what women can do and what will happen if you change the rules. But they get bundled together with claims about women’s proper role, so that defending the moral position also means defending a particular picture of the facts.

And that makes it harder to update. If acknowledging women’s capabilities threatens your justification for excluding them, then you have a motivation to discount the evidence. The broader lesson is that we should try to separate our values from the factual beliefs that conveniently support the institutions we’re accustomed to.
